DIES MONIES, Iowa. November l.
The silver lining of the rain clouds
that poured tons of water over each
Iowa acre during September will be
visible to farmers of the State when
next years crops are harvested.


A few weeks ago flooded streams
and inundated lowlands foretold huge
crop losses. But cheering state
ments from experienced observers
indicate that this years scattered
losses will be Offset by many indirect
benefits through the replenishing of
the water reservoir.


For many years the water reserve
has been depleted Scarcity Of top
soil water has interfered with crop
growth and the gradual lowering Of
the permanent ground water level has
caused shortage of well water.


This years rains came at season
when the crops were dormant. The
water thus penetrated the lower
levels, and also replenished the soH
water supply. 1t is estimated that
only about % per cent Of the precipi-
tation was carried off by the streams
and that the balance has SO saturated
the soil that the benefit will be
marked during the next growing sea-
son. and may be noticeable for the
next three or fo'lr years.

iron railing around a balcony outside

LET me loose, you fool! Let me

MEXICO CITY, December 9.-Pedro
Gual, Spanish charge d'affaires here,
was saved from possible serious injury
at the hands of an infuriated crowd
by Aaron Saenz, Mexican foreign min
lister, late yesterday. The Spanish
diplomat was being mauled mercilessly
by the crowd for striking a traffic
policeman in the face and knocking
him down because the policeman stop
ped his automobile for violating a
traffic rule.


Gual was driving his machine
through the commercial district dur
ing the peak of traffic and failed to
obey a stop signal. ,Thereupon the
policeman ran after the car, stopped
it and attempted to arrest Gual.


Indignant, Gual jumped out of the
car and struck the policeman in the
face. Passersby who had witnessed
the incident rushed to the rescue of
the officer and were showering blows
upon Gual when Senior Saenz happen
ed to come upon the scene.


The foreign minister, recognizing
the Spanish charge, rushed into the
vortex of the melee and loudly shout
ed to the crowd that the man they
were beating was a Spanish repre-
sentative to Mexico. Thereupon, the
hostile element Immediately ceased
their attack and Gual was taken away
from the scene.

James Mugford of the Continental
Navy was killed today in a hand-to-
hand action near Nantasket, which.
despite his death, resulted favorably
to the American cause. On the 18th
Capt. Mugford, in the Franklin, had
captured the British armed supply
ship Hope, and brought her safely
into this port directly under the eyes
of several enemy men.of-war This
morning, when he set out down the
bay in the Franklin in company with
the Lady Washington, commanded
by Capt. Cunningham. the enemy
followed in pursuit in 13 small boats.
and the Franklin's running aground
gave the Britishers a good oppor-
tunity of executing their plan


The Lady Washington came to
anchor near the Franklin when the
latter grounded, and the British small
boats appeared soon afterward. Capt.
Mugford hailed and received for ans
wer that they were from Boston. He
ordered them to keep off or he would
fire upon them. They begged him not
to fire, for they were going on board
him. Mugford instantly fired, and was
followed by all his men, then he
brought his broadside to bear and dis
charged his cannon loaded with
musket ball directly in upon them

Showing into first place few minutes

mile yacht race to Honolulu, Don
Lees 136-foot schooner, Invader, was
steadily lengthening her lead as the
six cOntenders for the Sir Thomas
Upton Cup dipped below the horizon.

yawl Poinzettia, dark horse in the
biennial yachting classic, while John
Barrymore's Mariner, which won the
Tahiti race last year and had been
picked as the favorite in the present
race, was q close third.

hind the Invader and the PoinZettia,
choosing a course because 1t led close

wind was stronger and less surface
current was encountered.

splitting tacks with the Mariner and
holding her own. The 40-foot schoon-
er. Jubillo, smallest craft in the fleet,

Invader. dropped ground rapidly to
the beat Of the turning mark at Point
Fermin, and then hauled on the star
board tack with the intention of pass
ing to the eastward of Catalina Is
land, instead of beating up to the
westward in the wake of the rest.

time across the channel, escorted by
a flock of sailing craft loaded with
friends, who were cheering the little
craft on.

craft until shortly before darkness
fell, when the entire fleet had passed
Catalina Island and entered the stiff
coastal northwest wind, which will

in Metropolitan New York seal them IN
such way that Tydol and Tydol alone

the sealed Tydol pump and the reasons

pers commended the move editorially.

vertising prize. The gasoline bootleg
gers were first resentful, then dismayed,
finally defeated. Today, New York City
gets clean, genuine high quality Tydol and
knows it.


Dealers demand sealed pumps


The effects of the sealed pump cam
paign were far reaching. From other
cities where there was not even a suspic-
ion of gasoline substitution, came the de-
mand of dealers and car owners for the
sealed pump. They wanted Tydol quail
ity given the additional protection Of
the sealed pump. They wanted to be sure
that substitution never could affect Tydol.

ducks they raised there.


The story is that one Winter "A
severe storm arose with SO much rain

together. The duck ponds became one
and the focks hopelessly mixed.


A riot almost resulted. The Chinese
duck keepers, excited lest they lose
their valuable birds, engaged i'll shrill
debates and blows were near. Then
an aged Chinese stepped into the surg

Let every one keep peace until
nightfall," he pleaded. when it is
dark, every duck will return to his
home flock"


1t was as the Chinese peacemaker
had claimed. When the sun went
down each duck returned to its
proper shed and was locked up, the
owners happy.


Since that day property values have
flown higher than ducks can wing and
the fashionable pleasure seekers are
for the most part unaware that
Waikiki ever was the breeding and
feeding ground of water fowl.

Following freakish radio reception

wore first noticed Thursday night,

displaying remarkable signal strength

unusual occurrence was noted Friday
and Saturday nights, with general
reception very poor and uncertain.

was at disadvantage, particularly Fri
day night, when effects Of the aurora

panies and press associations. The ad-
dress of President Coolidge, delivered

one Of the radio features that suffered
from q poor line, presumably caused
by the aurora


Similar occurrences in past years.
with both line telegraph and radio sig
nails, have led many prominent eng1-
neers to the belief that the northern
lights display has a direct influence
on the ether. The reason, however, is
generally regarded as great a mystery
as static.

spreading over the AlleShanies and

materials as their dresses. In one
New Hampshire family still lives an
old rag doll who for over 80 years has
plea sed it's daughters. True, she has
become somewhat the worse for wear,

renewed by the simple eXpedient of re-

ATLANTA. April 2S.-Irish clans
men from every part of the United
States and Canada gathered here to-
day to enact one of Americas Strang-
est funeral rites. The occasion was
the annual burial of the Irish horse
traders. held each April here for more
than % years.


Because of their wanderings, the
clans bury their dead only once a
year in order that all may be present
at the ceremony. They come-the
Rileys, O'Haras, CAROLS. Macks. Sher-
locks and other clans, bringing their
families with them.


Two members of the various clans
have died during the year past. Mrs.
Winnie Mack on June 20, and Pete
Carroll, on December II. The bodies
were sent here and have been held in
vaults until today.


After attending the burial the clans
depart for their far-scattered, posts,

When stocks the other day hit a

minating thing happened. Banks. in
surance companies and other conserv'
ative institutions holding large sums

psychology Of the moment and buy
or sell with their brains, not their
emotions.


Most spectators and investors, es-
pecially the little fellows, follow the
crowd. Thus they buy when stocks
are near the top and sell when they
are near the bottom and due for rise.
Successful purchasers buy low and
sell high. And when big, level-headed,
self-controlled people buy largely, 1t Is
a pretty good sign that the market
has reached bedrock.


The big ups and downs represent
emotional extremes and true values
are likely to be found somewhere near
the middle Of these big oscillations.

Francisco. and Russell Young of Cam
bridge. Mass: arrived here today on

Steamer Meanticut. which picked
them up after they had given up their
last hope and We're prepared for death


Hit Without Warning.


The hurricane hit the launch with

monster waves that time and again
smashed over the deck of the craft

water.

only reliance left to them was a jury
sail. rugged out of a blanket.

waves battering them.

1t was then that the Meanticut hove

death. for in his exhausted condition
he fell from the boarding ladder under
the sinking launch and was hauled
out with difficulty.

praise for Capt. S. G. Wallace and the
crew of the Menticut, who gave them
every care. furnished them clothing

BY the ASSOcldteu IIeSo'


LEWES, Del, April 14.-Historic
Cape Henlopen lighthouse, on the
Delaware Bay 9 miles south of
here. crumbled and toppled into the
sea yesterday afternoon.


A northeast gale--the longtime
enemy of the "Old Man of the Allan
tic," as the lighthouse was known
with the aid of an unusually high
tide, destroyed the pre-Revolutionary
structure. Henlopen was the second
oldest lighthouse on the Atlantic
coast. It was built by the British In
1865, a few years after the construc-
ton Of the light at Cape Henry:


For years the insecurity Of Hen
lopen light hid been apparent and
unusual efforts had been made to
preserve it for historic reasons. All
Monday night great waves from the
ocean ate into the sand foundation
at the foot of the ancient structure.
Harassed by the gale, the waves
pounded higher and higher until they
beat away the last supports and the
lighthouse tumbled over.


During the Revolutionary War, the
British seized Henlopen and burned
the interior. The United States
Government repaired the damage and
mounted a lens manufactured in
France whose rays were visible 40
miles at sea.


One Of the last dramas within sight
Of the lighthouse was during the
World War in 1918 when the oil
tanker William Pratt was sunk by a
U-boat. It's rays shone for the last
time on September 80, 1924. when
the Government opened a new steel
lighthouse nearby.

CAIRO, Egypt, April 6.-The Egyp-
tian government has organized relief
measures for the 1000 persons rem
dered homeless when fire swept the
village of Sagin-el-Kon, 6 miles from
Tantah.


At least 35 persons perished in the
fire, which started at noon Saturday
when a sudden change in the wind
carried sparks from a household fire,
kindled outside the dwelling, to the
straw-covered roof.


The flames spread with appalling
rapidity, from 200 to 800 dwellings
being ablaZe within few minutes.
The villagers rushed wildly to and
fro seeking escape from the burning
mass. Many of those cut off were
women and children.


Fire brigades from nearby towns
arrived, but were unable to control
the fire until Sunday morning, when
practically the entire village had been
leveled. Thirty-five bodies were found
in the debris. Many Of those who es-
capped were badly burned.


The government has supplied tents
and flour for the homeless. Village
fires in Egypt are generally caused, as
in this case, by change in the wind
sending sparks from domestic fires to
the highly infiammable roofs.

DEARBORN, Mich, December 25-
Santa Claus, who it appears is very
dear friend Of Henry Ford. held open
house just on the eve Of Christmas
day to the delight and surprise of
100 little boys and girls.


Escorted by Ford and his wife, the
little folk drove through the sparkling
darkness Of night over a rough and
tree-bordered path to the workshop of
Santa Claus on the Ford estate here
And there was the smiling old fellow
with long white beard, and dressed in
heavy furs. ready to receive the party
under a great Christmas tree spar
king with lights.


The old fellow, who knew most of
the youngsters by name, led them into
his two-room log home where a work
bench stood loaded with nearly
finished toys. Every bench, chair,
and rack was burdened with dolls,
drums, mechanical toys, candy canes
and all that makes Christmas happy
for the little people.


Wide-eyed with wonder the children
wandered about the shop receiving
presents from Santa himself, who
promised that he would visit them
again Christmas morning early.

Boys and girls who love dogs and
are eager to have one of their own
probably do not realize that there
are 1ss different kinds of them.


Learned men who study animals
say that one kind of dog is different
from another chiefly in regard to the
form and size of it's ears. According
to this standard they have grouped
all the different kinds Of dogs into
six classes.


The first of these includes the wolf
dogs. They are large. rather wild
animals living in the northern coun-
tries, and generally have big bushy
tails. They are used by the people
Of these lands to draw their sleds
over the snow and ice.


Sheep dogs are common in coun-
tries where sheep are raised In large
numbers. They are used to guard the
fiocks and keep away other animals,
but they are really members Of the
wolf dog class themselves.

Dogs belonging to the greyhound
class are known to have existed
1000 years ago in Egypt. They are
delicate creatures. long of leg and
ver;' swift in running.


Spaniels, which form the third group,
are smaller. and have long silky
hair and big hanging ears. Hounds are
characterized by long, ears. short hair
and long muZZles. They are favorites
of men all over the world for hunting.


Mastiffs, in which class are bull
dogs and pugs, are very strong and
very brave. Their jaws are heavy
and powerful and their bodies are
stocky.


The terrier, the last class. is one
of the oldest known kinds of dog.
They are small dogs and are largely
used for the destruction of such ami
mails as rats, otters and weasels-a
sport which they seem to enjoy
greatly.

! If you're the golden-haired darling
| of a large and devoted family, you're
a very lucky girl in one way. There's
| nothing more satisfying and comfort
| ing in the world than the knowledge
that no matter what blows you may
| receive from the rest Of the world, one
group at home thinks you're the

But the girl who depends too much
on her loving family's support Is apt

| social Whirl."


kids, and had a large and adoring
| family from the minute she arrived
on earth.


They were none of them very good
looking or clever, so when Helene ar
| rived with her lovely golden hair,
they united in praising the great
beauty who had come to make the
family happy.


Then at school Helene did pretty
well. She got better marks than most
of the older brothers and sisters had
been able to achieve.
She did nothing really extraordi-
| nary, but her fond parents and other
relatives were hugely impressed with
her every action.
In this way she arrived at her 18th
year with the conviction that she was
beautiful, talented, witty and, oh, so
charming.


1t wasn't her fault, you see. She
had it dinned into her ears so long
that she was perfect riot, she SIM
ply awaited the coming of social sue
cess with all the confidence in the
world.


On the night of her first big dance,
mother and sister and the boys came
in and raved ecstatically over the
slim, green dance frock.
Good Lord, you'll have a wonder
full time" sighed Doris. her sister
You're just made to be popular"
And when Helene arrived at the big
Jig she never even noticed how much
more sophisticated and charming the
other girls looked.


She never realized that she looked
rather homemade and dolly beside the
smart young things who were old
timers at these dances.


She took an awful beating that
night as the dreary evening wore on.
and no one cut in-no one asked to
see her again-no one but her suffer-
ing partner even knew she was there.


Still the conceit which her loved
ones had planted in her mind refused
to die.


She went through several painful
years trying to make herself believe
that the outside world didn't appreci-
ate real beauty and wit and charm.


Then she finally came down off her
high horse and strove desperately to
learn how to be smart and clever and
bright, just like all the other girls she
met when she went out.


It's unwise to rely on the love-blind-
ed eyes Of adoring familie~ for clear
vision as to our true worth.


Don't bank too much on the opin.
ion of the family when you go out to
face the cruel world-be it business
or social.


Your mother and father may think
you've got everybody else cleaned off
the map, but their ideas won't inf1u-
ence the stag line one way or the
other.

beyond Darlington.

WIGGINS, Miss, October 2S.-In
that section OF Mississippi where the
tall long-leaf pine casts it's shadow on
the hillsides. busy fingers are picking,
sorting and polishing the long pine
needles to be made into gift baskets
and other art objects for the Christ
mas trade.


Vases. baskets, floor lamps. jewel
casketS and boxes of various types
are woven from the homely pine nee-
dies. Thousands of dollars were
brought into the State last year by
what has become known as the fire
side industry" and woman members
of county demonstration clubs who
have become experts at the art were
unable to fill all orders.


The demand for the woven objects
has lifted the work from a pastime,
furnishing club members with pin
money" into an actual commercial
class. The work is distributed among
members and the proceeds are divided
according to the time and work put
in. With materials free, all of the in
come Is clear profit.


Weaving of native materials began
during the war between the States,
when manufactured articles were
scarce ana the need for them great.
Mrs. J. M. McAfee of West Point, Ca,
who made both hats and baskets. was
credited with having originated the
work.

put in its first appearance in Chicago
today and went the way of beverages

but tested herds.

favorably.

$4,000 in the Chicago district alone.

culin-tested herds has resulted in q

sin. whose cows have not met the
test.

While passing the home of an ac-
quaintance several months ago, the
garden editor was asked to look at
some apple trees and the Japanese
Burning Bush (Euonymus japonica)
which were not in a thrifty condition.
An inspection showed that all the
plants were infested with scale in
Sects.


There are several types of this pest
the San Jose scale, the oyster shell
scale and the scurfy scale. The in
dividual scales are about the size of a


pin-head and are somewhat raised in


the center. With the point of knife


they can be tipped back. exposing the
organism. When abundant the scales
literally incrust the limbs and


branches, giving an ashgray appear
ance. They damage fruit trees and


shrubs by sucking the sap from the


tissues of the plants.


These pests are successfully con-
trolled by the annual use of very
strong sprays-either the Winter
strength of lime-sulphur spray or one
of the miscible oils--applied during


the dormant season. Inspect your
trees and shrubs for scales, and spray
during the next few weeks.

KINGSTON. II. l.. June 26.-Three
railroad employees were killed today
when the boiler of a locomotive haul

over marshland near here. The
wreckage OF the freight train was
thrown onto the passenger tracks and
a few minutes later the New York,
New Haven and Hartford's Cape
Colder" from New York for Cape
Cod points, crashed into the wreck
age.


The locomotive of the passenger
train was thrown from the rails and
the first car dived into the swamp.
Several passengers were slightly hurt.
The fact that none was seriously in
jured is believed to have been due
to the fact that none of the upper
berths on the flyer was occupied. The
train, which runs only on Saturday
mornings. was making its first trip
of the sea son.


The dead:


William Moulton, engineer of the
freight.


George Hathaway. fireman.


James J. Muvaney. a spare man,
riding in the cab of the freight loco
motive.


The engineer of the express train
was injured.


The boiler of the freight locomotive
was hurled many feet into the swamp.
Many of the shattered cars of the
freight were filed with finished cloth
and with bundles of American flags
being shipped from the textile cities
for the July 4 celebration. For a
great distance the track was strewn
with oilbedraggled flags and bolts OF
cloth.

been determined.

By the Associated Press.


CHICAGO, September 25.-The
North and Middle West shivered to.
day In the swirl of wintry blasts
sweeping in a broad southeasterly fan
from snow-capped wheat fields on
the western Canadian prairies.


To the south the cold wave moved
down the lower Ohio Valley and into
the Texas Panhandle. while the winds
that halted wheat harvesting in
Alberta. Manitoba and Saskatchewan
along the st. Lawrence toward the
seaboard.


The unreasonable temperatures sent
the mercury scurrying downward to
unprecedented September levels and
brought well below freezing weather
to many northwestern points.


Apple Crop Suffers.


In the American Northwest the
wave assumed proportions unparalleled
in the meteorological records and
threatened extensive damage to apple
and other crops in Washington and
Oregon.


From that area a blighting chill
crept over fields Of corn and standing
small grain in the Central West, add
ing to the millions Of dollars damage
from recent heavy rains. In Western
plain fields not reached by snow
fiurries, killing frosts were spread.


Damage to unharvested crops was
estimated at $l2. 0o0, 900.


Farmers in Illinois and Iowa We're
spurred to activity in sodden fields by
warnings to recover seed corn from
their crop. While Kansas corn was
reported generally beyond the danger
point, there was grave fear to the
eastward that the cold and frost wind,
In many instances, complete the dam
age begun by a record September
rainfall.


Winds of tornado velocity carried
the lower temperatures to many re-
gions, and central Illinois, weary from
three weeks unceasing battle with
floods, watched new rain start streams
backing up toward overflow stages.


A record low temperature OF 90
above was reported from Yakima
Wash, and Baker, Greg, while the
eastern end of the wave had sent the
mercury to Al degrees at Chicago
early today. Snow fiurries were re.
ported in northern Illinois, Iowa and
Minnesota.


The coolest reported spot In the
country was Helena, Mont, where
thermometers read 6 degrees above
zero. Ankle-deep snow was reported
in parts of the Dakotas, with tempera
lures dropping as much as 40 degrees
in few hours.


Slowly rising temperatures were
forecast over much of the Middle West
today, with cloudy skies and possible
thunderstorms.


Oil Derricks Felled.


PETROLIA, Ont, September "a
R.-aigh winds and torrential rains
swept this district with hurricane
violence yesterday wrecking houses
topping oil derricks and disrupting
telegraph and telephone communica.
ton.


The storm was the worst the district
has ever experienced. In one of the
oil fields near here, all the derricks
were felled. An automobile truck was
blown from the highway.


The reports from Winnipeg said
the storm, which brought some snow
and rain to the prairie provinces dur
ing the last three days, passed east
ward last night. leaving damage that
will run into millions of dollars to
the unharvested crops in Manitoba,
Alberta and Saskatchewan.


The passage of the storm carried
the first snow of the season into West
ern Ontario. Port Arthur reported d
light snowfall.

ans terrified face could be seen

clutchinE her purse desperately Be

Press that he saw the plane burst
into flames near the tail when about
400 feet in the air 1t dived to earth
The crash was followed by two ex

and making it impossible to rescue the
passengers, who. were piled in a heap

was thrown several feet in front of

death.


The weather was perfect and the
cause of the accident had not been
determined tonight.


The tragedy Is the second cross

two months. a plane en- route from,

others were injured in this crash. The
plane was a sister ship to the plane

ALBANY, N. Y, April 27.--Resi-
dents of northeastern New York
State breathed easier today with
Adirondack streams reported either
near their food peaks or slowly re-
ceding. The Saranac and Black Riv.
ers, worst offenders during the past
few days, rose slowly yesterday, but
last night the Black River had reached
it's peak and the Saranac River had
become sluggish even in its lower
reaches.


Watertown suffered its greatest loss
from the flood through the shutting
down of factories getting their power
from the Black River. Trolley service
there, interrupted during the morn.
ing, was resumed later in the day.


Despite a slight drop in temperature
and lack Of sunshine, the Saranac
increased in volume enough to over.
flow the highway at several points
and some families living on valley
farms are reported to have been driv-
en- from their homes by the rising
water.


At Albany the Hudson River, after
holding almost steady yesterday, again
was rising last night under the first
flow of a fourfoot crest far upstream.

vessel In momentary danger of found
ering-superstructur boats and bridge
smashed, and two holds and the en-
gine room flooded.

Aldworth in answer to distress signals,
but the captain and crew refused to
leave the Aldworth. Finally, after
hours of anxiety and peril, the sea
abated and the Aldworth got under
way toward Queenstown, conveyed by
the American steamer West Eldara.


The Aldworth, a steel vessel of
1859 tons. left Norfolk for Queens
town November 4.

Safety in driving depends in large
measure upon the motorists recogni-
ton of the hazards offered by various
types of streets. it is pointed out by
agencies cooperating in the reduction
of traffic accidents.


The following street types are listed
as those which the motorist should
know the moment his car is turned
into one:


a. Wide streets and narrow streets.


b. Asphalt, brick. wood block
macadam. sandy. clay and dirt streets
wet or dryl.


c. Busy streets, idle streets.


q. Streets with car tracks.


g. Boulevards and ordinary traffic
streets


f. Dusty streets


9. Streets with curves and blind
corners.


Drivers should appreciate the haz
ards resulting from such conditions
and govern themselves accordingly.


Generally speaking, wide streets are
safer than narrow streets. They offer
greater space in which drivers can
operate in their endeavors to avoid
running into persons, objects and
other vehicles.


Asphalt, brick. wood block maca dam.
sa ndy. cla- and dirt streets each have
different characteristics that may
affect safe driving. Rain and snow
make still further changes in the
character of streets.


Wood swells when wet. Wood block
streets. therefore, should be watched
carefully The uneven swelling of
blocks may result in dangerous
bumps and holes.


Moisture forms a thin film over
wood blocks and makes them un.
usually slippery.

BY Cable to The Star and Chicago Daily News.
LONDON, May S.-Except for the
fact that traffic is more congested
than usual, no visitor would realize
! that London is gripped by a general
strike.


Nearly a million cars. from anti
quated two-cylinder Napiers to latest
type Rolls Royce, most of them bear
ing the legend I'VE will give you a
lift are on the streets. Motor lOr-
ries have been transformed into tenn
porary busses displaying huge signs
| reading, Ladies first"


The endeavor to maintain conf
| munication with the suburban dis
tricts involves some risk, for az soon
as the metropolitan area Is left be-
hind young strikers are encountered
who spend their time trying to block
trathc. occasionally mishandlinS
drivers and burning cars when no
strong police force is in sight.
Ex-Army Officers Help.


Here and there buses belonging to
the General Omnibus Co. may be
seen driven by volunteer chauffeurs,
with sturdy policemen armed with
clubs and pistols sitting next to the
conductors.


Regular skeleton services are kept
going on the main subway lines, but
the task Is difficult since the volun-
teers are mostly ex-army officers.
who have had little experience driv-
ing complicated electrical engines.


The London middle class has an
swered the governments call for vol
unteers the same way they answered
kitchener's appeal in 1914. Recruit
ing stations are working overtime en-
listening men and women.


All Classes Help.


Milk wagons are being driven by
pretty society girls, while retired gen.
erals and wealthy young men about
town are weighing out flour, unload
ing milk from the few trains arriv-
ing. carrying mail sacks, and stocking
engines which are driven by super
intendents and chief engineers of the
railway companies.


Its the best holiday I've had in
years and it does me a lot of good"
said young Earl Percy, heir of the
Duke of northumberland, who was
found rolling huge milk cans from a
lorry into the storehouse in Hyde
Park.

Those who predicted radio broad
casting would kill the newspaper
proved false prophets. London Is suf-
fering acutely from It's lack OF news
papers. Hand-prnted bulletins and
typewriter sheets are sold for any
thing from pence to 6 pence ana are
snapped up quickly.


More than q million radio sets have
been installed in houses and offices
since Saturday. but the dry, sparse
communiques broadcast by the gov
ernment six times a day have failed
to satisfy the populace.


Bicycles I'm Demand.


While the principal industries are
suffering extremely serious losses
some minor industries are reaping
rich harvests. The Coventry bicycle
factories are working overtime and
still are unable to satisfy the demand
for bikes. Secondhand automobiles,
for which dealers would have been
glad to get 5000 last week. are bring
ing two or three times that sum.


London life, however. goes on as
usual. The theaters continue to run
before half-empty houses. Patrons
tend. Night life in the smart restau





before.


Rows Of expensive cars parked in
front of the leading hotels and 1clubs
give the impression that the country
is more prosperous than ever.


Danger Still Exists.


The picture is very different. how
ever, in the suburbs, where crowds
of poorly dressed, sullen.faced men
look anything but contented.


The danger of serious conflicts has
not been averted. Both strike lead
ers and authorities are doing their
utmost to prevent serious clashes. but.
as one leader said. there are fools
who may spill the beans in both
camps" The writer has heard many
intelligent men who are backing the
government say. The government
ought to shoot the blighters." On
the other hand. many strikers believe
the movement: will fail unless blood
is shed" This is the great danger
England is facing now. If some rash
step is taken by irresponsible mem
bers of either side the consequences
will be incalculable.

Mrs. Morrow was the most envied
and the most admired woman in Co
lumbia. Yet she was neither young
nor beautiful. neither rich nor ac-
complished. She was. however, that
remarkable thing which we seldom
sea radiant woman.


She had come to Columbia for a
few casual weeks .one Summer, had
fallen in love with it, bought a home
for herself and stayed. The small
white. house back from the broad vii
lage street was charmingly modest,
and quite big enough for its single oc-
cupant and the guests she chose to
have there. Mrs. Morrow made no
display; she bought comfortable furni-
ture for her house, which she ar
ranged with taste. She had brought
nothing with her, not even a few
books, though she was fond of read
ing and soon had a we'll stocked book
case.


Everybody except Miss Podd accept
ed her on the instant, but then Miss
Podd never accepted anybody. She
was all the time studying Mrs. Nor
row, trying to get at her history.


There's something about her." she
said. shaking her head.


THAT you don't like?" asked Mrs.
Rose quickly.


II won't say that. There's some.
thing about her that-baffles me-"


Naomi Podd, you are a regular
Paul Pry in petticoats," laughed Mrs.
Rose. She was one of the few people
who could say what they thought to
Miss Podd.


Mrs. Morrow stirred things up in
Columbia. She gave afternoon teas,
for which she made the cakes, and
card parties and she had. people in to
dinner frequently. She seemed never
to get enough Of sociability and she
entertained delightfully."- But while she
was friendly with everybody she gave
no one her inmost confidence. One
felt, like Miss Podd, that she withheld
good deal. though she apparently
told everything about herself. She had
married young, her husband had lived
nine years, she had child and lost it,
and she wasn't anchored fast to any
particular place on earth. She liked
Columbia, and she was going to stay
there If the people would let her.


There was no doubt about their
wanting her to stay when she gave
them all such good times. Neighbor-
illness was an instinct with her, it
seemed; she "neighbored" everybody.
She had nothing that was not at the
command of her friends at any time
And her radiance made her refreshing
as q bunch of flowers or a ray of
sunshine wherever she went


Her radiance made people envy
while they admired her. She was all
joy, all good health, all sweetness.
Her eyes shone, her lips smiled, she
laughed like chime of silver bells.
she could tell the funniest stories you
ever heard and she could find fun
everywhere. Nothing so bright or
Frightening as she had even been in
Columbia. One forgot that she
weighed 1870 pounds and had not a
good figure, that her hair was gray

MOSCOW, April 24.-The Moscow

suburban villages are under water.

part of the city lying along It's banks

Kremlin.

have been forced to abandon their
homes. Throughout the night boats
bearing torches presented g. fantastic
sight on the river and its tributaries
as rescue parties moved hither and
thither to take n1arooned families to
higher ground. Likewise pontoon bat
talionS were buGly engaged in res
cuing peasants and their cattle.


Field kitchens have been established
at various points to feed homeless per
sons, and military barracks have been
opened to give them shelter. Scores

Bridge are flooded. Firemen In boats
rescued the occupants

ing, reaching the 29-foot level, A
heavy rain increased the rapidity with

Philadelphia.

CLINTON, n. j., December o.
Two brothers and their sister, who for
II hours withstood the attack of 80
State troopers on their farmhouse at
the foot of Jugtown Mountain at Jut-
land near here, were captured today
when the officers made concerted
rush on the house.


James and Beatrice Meaney were
slightly. wounded by the fire which
the troopers poured into the rambling
old house throughout the night in re.
ply to volleys from the occupants.
Timothy .Meaney was uninjured. The
three offered no resistance when the
troopers broke into the house.


The fight between the farmers and
officers started yesterday afternoon
when two agents for the Society for
the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals
went to the farm to investigate com.
plants of mistreatment of cattle. The
brothers refused to allow the agents
to inspect the stock and they obtained
a. search warrant.


Troopers expressed surprise that
the three had been able to withstand
the effects of tear gas bombs which
were hurled into the house during the
night.


Larson, State trooper. who went
with officers to serve the warrant. was
ordered off by James, who held a shot.
gun. He and the agents backed away
and when, about 80 feet off Larson
fred, striking James in the kneecap.


Timothy rushed into the house and
obtained another shotgun, which he
fired at Larson.


Corpl. Matthew Daily arrived with
reinforcements. Daily and Larson
smashed in a door and entered. A
shotgun was pushed throug a door,
according to Daily, and both barrels
were discharged at him. He fired
and then retired. Timothy opened
fire from the kitchen window and the
troopers returned a volley.


DAILY was struck as he started to
walk across the yard. Trooper Peter
Smith also was wounded Early this
morning 80 troopers rushed the house
and hurled eight tear gas bombs
through the windows.


There was a lull in the firing for
three hours and then Timothy shout
ed: Don't throw any more bombs.
The other two are dead Six troopers
forced their way into the kitchen and
disarmed him. James and Beatrice
were found in another room. Beatrice
was wounded in the hip.

being summoned by a neighbor
woman, who heard the commotion.

on which Kraft had loaned money
Christmas eve, had been torn from
his finger.


Examiners declared the murder
another Apache crime.

In the soft mucky ground among
the alders the bloodroot has come up
near my house. and these days every
one who lives even just a little way
out of the city has seen 1t, rising pale
and starry from the earth. No mat
ter how early ! get up l always hnd
the bloodroot blossoms wide blown.
But in the last light of the April sun
sets they generally close up-little
white balls of flowers. They tell the
time of day as surely as the distant
blowing of the evening whistles does.


Bloodroot they call it, this stainless
white flower. If you break the stem
you will soon know why, for a pale
red juice exudes swiftly from the
plant and stains your fingers orange.
Brightest of all are the colors that
flow from the rootstock itself, and 1t
is said that Indians smeared their
faces with this Stair before they took
the warpath.


Almost more lovely than the flow
ers themselves are the bloodroot
leaves that shoot up from the earth
beside the flower stems. and stand
curled like banners yet furled. Slow
ly they open out, pale green and
thick, with a faint bloom on them
and a feeling like the touch Of soft
leather.


After the flowers have come and
gone the leaves will grow larger and
larger, and then in late Summer will
die away and all trace of the blood
roots position will be lost, SO that If
you want to find the root stocks in
the Fall you will have to mark the
spot now while you can find 1t. The
bloodroot is our only native repre-
sentative Of the beautiful, curious
poppy family.

RENO, New, August 17.-Discov-
cry OF a miniature volcano In the
Modoc lava beds Of northeastern
California, about $50 miles northwest
Of Reno. coupled with increasing &C.
tivity in the huge boiling springs
| north and south Of this city, has re-
vfved interest among scientists in the
possibilities Of eruptions along the
eastern flank Of the Sierra Nevada
Mountains.


The volcanic vent found emitting
steam and smoke In the Modoc region
evidently Is the tiny crater Of q
tremendous volcano which desolated
the area. centuries ago. The country
for miles around Is covered deeply
with lava and pumice stone. resem-
bling the desolate region around
Mount Lassen, the only active vol
cano on the North American main
land.


Springs Snort Steam.


The sulphurous. boiling springs in
the Steamboat Springs field. less than
ing new activity, spraying out steam
and columns of scalding water. A
heavy haze of sulphurous gas hangs
over the Kissing vent. At Gerlach,
$50 miles north of this city, huge
scalding springs are snorting steam
and noxious vapors. The entire
mountainous belt from Steamboat
Springs to Mount LaSsen shows pro.
nounced indications of subterranean
disturbances. with possibilities of vol
canic eruptions.


Underground reservoirs of scalding
water many years ago halted develop.
ment of the silver mines on the Com
stock Lode at Virginia City and have
since defeated efforts to work the
deep-seated ore deposits. Hot springs
abound throughout northwestern Ne
vada and adjacent California and
Oregon counties, and a distinct vol
canic belt has been located by recent
Investigations.


After slumber1ng for centuries
Mount Lassen broke into spectacular
activity IL years ago, overwhelming
fertile areas with mud and sulphurous
vapors. The mountain has emitted
ashes, hot mud and clouds of steam
at intervals ever since, its activity
being particularly marked after heavy
storms. Scientists express the belief
that Lassen may again burst into
flaming vigor whenever the vents con-
stituting its safety valves become
choked or whenever water from
heavy SHOWS penertateS its interior.


The kissing, steaming vents and
bubbling hot springs show that sub
terranean fires still rage underneath
the entire region along the northeast
ern slope Of the Sierr'as.

line. conspired merely TO make the
outing cooler.

then six kegs Of ice cream for the

PENSACOLA, Fla, Sept. 3D.
This city, shut off from the outside
world for three days while the
West Indian hurricane dashed the
Gulf Coast, resumed business as
usual today while preparations were
made to repair the havoc.


With no lives lost, and none re-
ported injured, Pensacola, considered
itself lucky that it weathered the
hurricane with less than 100000
damage, most Of which was done to
public utilities, such as wharves,
docks, telephone, railroad and power
companies.


Pensacola received ample warn
ing Of the coming Of the hurricane
and made its preparations accord.
ingly. Business was suspended at
the first rise in the wind, people
locked themselves in their houses
and waited patiently for the gale
to cease.


In less than two hours after the
storm passed, citizens drained the
water from their streets and took
a survey of the damage. Very lit
tie private property was destroyed.
although a few small houses were
unroofed.


A relief train dispatched here
from Tallahassee turned back when
it was found that Pensacola needed
no help.

constipated. The bowels may

tial. Enough old matter is left to
form gas, hinder digestion and

LONDON, January 5.-More British
peerages became extinct in 1925 than
in any twentieth century year except
1915. The new edition of De Brett'S,
the standard compilation of the
realms nobility, records the extinc-
ton of nine titles above the baronetcy
rank. The outstanding case is that
brought about by the death of Mar
quis Curzon of Kedleston, which
wiped out both the marquisate and
earldom Of that name. The Ribbles-
dale baronetcy, dating from 1897,
passed with the death Of Lord Rib
blesdale, his son and heir having been
killed in the war. and the Rawlinson
baronetcy became extinct with the
death Of Gen. Lord Rawlinson.


The new De Brett contains five
new peerages, conferred during 1925,
the recipients being the Earl of Ok.
ford and Asquith, Baron Bradbury,
Baron Lloyd, Baron Merrivale and
Baron Stonehaven.

BY the Associated Press.


LONDON, December 18.-The crisis
caused yesterday by the military coup
d'etat directed by Gen. Smetona has
come to an end, says message re-
ceived today from Kovno by the Lithu-
anian legation.


The message stated that President
Grinius, after accepting the resigna-
ion of the Slezevicius cabinet, resumed
his normal duties in Kovno. He has
appointed Prof. Valdemaras, premier
and minister of foreign affairs, and
other Nationalists as members of the
new cabinet. These include Col.
Merkys as minister of defense and
DIR. Kervelis as minister of finance.


One report, through Warsaw, says
there was fighting on Green Hill, near
Kovno, where one regiment remained
loyal to the government.


With only erratic telephone and tele-
graph communication the situation
was not entir ely clear today, but it
seemed established that a group head
ed by former President Antona
Smetona and Maj. Plekhavichus was
in the saddle, welding dictatorial
power and with the army behind it..


The leaders of the coup charged that
the old government under the mode
rate Socialist premier, M. Elezevicius,
had betrayed Lithuania to the Bolshe-
visits and to foreign nations. They
are said to have been particularly dis
satisfied with the governments le'
nient attitude toward Poland and other
bordering states.


Advices indicate that Gen. Smetona
win make the question of the Wilma
district prominent part of the new
regimes political program. This dis
triet, formerly part of Russia, was
awarded to Poland by the allied coun-
Gil of ambassadors, but Lithuania
has refused to recognize the ambassa-
doris decision.


The present revolt, after lengthy
secret preparation, was launched in
the small hours of yesterday morning.
The Diet was at the fag end of a long
night session when troops entered.
The commanding officer, Maj. Plekha-
vichus, mounted the speakers tri-
bune, announced that the Diet was
dissolved and it's officers under ar
rest, and that the army had assumed
authority.

Blanche Solomon, years old. was

Other members of the Solomon
household, at 1912 Thirteenth street,
probably owe their lives to the little


girls pet kitten, Grapes, who
aroused her uncle Dy clawing at his
face.


The uncle, Meyer Rosenblatt, and
little Blanche were sleeping in the
same room when fire started at about
$3.50 am. Mr.. Rosenblatt rushed to the
other rooms to awaken his parents,
Mr.. and Mrs. Gabriel Rosenblatt; MIR.

Then he rushed back to get Blanche.
but flames blocked his path. The
older survivors were forced to jump
from second.Story front windows into
the arms of neighbors, after tossing
Sylvia to safety from the same place.
All slightly burned or injured by
the jump. the dazed families watched
while firemen subdlsed the flames.
Then the search for Blanche began.
Curled Up Under Bed.
They found her curled up beneath
her Grandfather Rosenblatt's bed, as
though seeking protection from the
soaring flames that closed in upon
her. Awakened by the frantic screams
of parents and other relatives, APP
parently, the child had battled her
way through the burning hall to her
grandfa theirs room. With escape
through the windows blocked, she
probably had crawled under the bed,
thinking it would halt the fires prog
ress until help arrived.


nj - -
Blanche's body to Emergency Hos
pital, but physicians there said life
was extinct. Gabriel Rosenblatt, the
grandfather, was treated for burned
arms. and Mrs. Soloman, the mother,
was cut and bruised. Young Rosen-
blatt was slightly burned. After re.
ceiving medical attention, all went to
the home of relatives few blocks
away.


Tomorrow was to have been a gala
day in the Solomon home. It will be
Sylvia's fourth birthday. Blanche
passed her sixth just a few days ago,
and dual celebration in honor of the
two great events was to have been
held. A big cake was ready and little

But those playmates who call will 60

Store Escapes Flames.
The rear of the house was nearly
destroyed by the fire and most of the
front was damaged. The store on the
first floor escaped with only damage
by water. The flames ate their way
through a wall into the neighboring
home of Charles Gerson, a tailor.
The blaze there was checked. how
ever, before it did much damage.
What became of Grapes? Well, no


member of the family knows yet.
Some persons remembered seeing the
kitten leave the house and prowl
among the crowd until Blanche's body
was discovered. Then Grapes disap-
peared, only to revisit the scene of


the tragedy for brief moment later
in the morning and then again to
leave.
